subject: design-technology
title: Foundations: Hardwoods and Softwoods
welcome_lead: Step into the timber yard and learn the difference between hardwoods and softwoods.
meta_desc: Learn hardwood and softwood examples and properties for GCSE Design & Technology.
final_note: You can classify timbers as hardwood or softwood and match them to uses.

concepts.def: Tough hardwood used in furniture and flooring.
Affordable softwood widely used in joinery.
Very light hardwood used in modelling.

walkthroughs.body_html: The labels hardwood and softwood are botanical, not about hardness. Hardwoods come from broadleaf deciduous trees that grow slowly; softwoods come from fast-growing conifers. Most hardwoods are dense, but balsa is a hardwood that is famously light.

walkthroughs.h2: Hardwoods and softwoods you must know
walkthroughs.body_html: Hardwoods: oak, mahogany, beech, ash, balsa. Softwoods: pine, spruce, larch, cedar. Each has typical uses — oak for sturdy furniture, pine for construction, cedar for outdoor cladding because of natural oils that resist rot.

walkthroughs.h2: Choosing wood for a kitchen worktop
walkthroughs.body_html: A worktop needs hardness and water resistance. Beech or oak (hardwoods) outperform pine (softwood) because their dense grain resists knife marks and stains, especially when sealed with oil.

mcqs.q: What determines whether a timber is a hardwood or softwood?
options: Whether the wood itself is physically hard or soft.
How long the tree took to grow.
The type of tree - deciduous (hardwood) or coniferous (softwood), not its hardness.
